A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning and are readable throughout, including equations, tables and figures. V1's Appendices A–C can be compared with v2's revised main text; v2 contains no appendices. The substantial revisions do not prevent reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original DNAR experiments on SALSA-CLRS and CLRS-30 in Tables 1–2, together with discretization ablation, sequential-training and no-hint BFS findings.

after.justification: V2 reports original DNAR benchmark results in Tables 1–2, retained ablation and no-hint findings, and additional multitask experiments.

M1.justification: V1's additive scalar attention bias becomes min/max-indicator augmentation of attention keys in v2 Section 3.3. V2 also changes node/edge update inputs, uses a virtual node and one attention head per scalar, and replaces the parameter-free scalar scattering of v1 Appendix C with learned inc/keep/push operations. Training now uses scalar MSE and type-specific hint losses instead of v1's all-state cross-entropy formulation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six SALSA-CLRS algorithms and the same four corresponding CLRS-30 tasks; no-hint experiments remain BFS-only. Multitask training combines retained coverage. V2's 'Maximum Independent Set' wording does not establish a different task from v1's SALSA-CLRS maximal independent set experiment.

E2.justification: V2 adds Triplet-GMPNN to the four-task CLRS-30 comparison in Table 2. GIN and PGN remain the SALSA-CLRS comparators, and Hint-ReLIC and G-ForgetNet remain in Table 2.

E3.justification: V2 introduces joint training of a shared processor with task-specific encoders/decoders, accumulating gradients across tasks for 10,000 optimization steps. The stated single-task learning rate changes from 0.0003 to 0.001, while batch size 32 and 1,000 steps remain. V1's separate sequential-training setup using smaller graphs and trajectory-weighted hint losses is no longer reported.

E4.justification: V1 Section 5.5's analysis of sequential-training sensitivity and its mitigation through loss weighting and smaller training graphs is removed. The discretization-removal ablation and the no-hint BFS analysis of state usage and failure beyond learned distance layers are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed averages, omit standard deviations in Table 1 and present uncertainty values in Table 2. The added comparator follows the existing reporting practice; no new statistical estimation or multitask-specific uncertainty procedure is stated.

E6.justification: V2 adds the substantive finding that one jointly trained processor achieves perfect generalization across all covered algorithms. Table 2 additionally reports Triplet-GMPNN node scores of 99.73, 47.79, 96.05 and 86.39 for BFS, DFS, Dijkstra and MST-Prim. All existing numerical entries in Tables 1–2 are unchanged, while v1's successful sequential-training finding is removed. The new findings concern additional settings, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The mathematical basis of the attention-correctness argument changes: v1 Section 6 invokes bounded scalars and sufficiently separated state priorities, whereas v2 Section 5 invokes finite checks of how min/max indicators affect attention weights. V2 Section 3.4 also introduces explicit node/edge scalar recurrences with binary inc/keep/push functions, replacing the task-specific scalar construction and invariant in v1 Appendix C.

C1.justification: V2 expands the abstract and introduction's empirical contribution to perfect generalization in both single-task and multitask setups, specifically claiming that one network executes all covered algorithms. V1's headline result concerns separately learned algorithmic tasks. The central interpretability and correctness claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 Section 7 adds concrete qualifications: hard attention cannot compute a neighborhood mean in one step, some CLRS-30 hint transitions therefore exceed the current architecture's expressivity, and correct convergence is not guaranteed for every initialization or training distribution. Existing no-hint interpretations and most future-work discussion remain, while the explanation of sequential-training difficulties is removed.

D1.justification: V2 adds learned-gate implementation details, multitask gradient accumulation, A100 hardware and training times below one hour for single-task and 5–6 hours for multitask learning. It omits v1 Appendix B's explicit state vocabularies and sampling/sequential-training details, and replaces Appendix C's task-specific scalar instructions with a general updater specification. The same code link moves from Appendix A to a footnote.

R1.justification: V2 adds Georgiev et al. (2021), Algorithmic Concept-Based Explainable Reasoning, and removes the Prim (1957) reference. The broader research positioning remains similar. Changes to the Recursive Algorithmic Reasoning, Tracr, RASP-L and GIN references identify existing works through updated bibliographic information.

P1.justification: V2 removes the standalone Learning section and its three learning-mode subsections, condenses training into Experiments, substantially shortens task descriptions and reorders the experimental subsections. It also restructures the introduction around three building blocks and separates limitations from future work. Appendix content is partly relocated or replaced and partly omitted.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main document from two columns to a predominantly single-column layout and adds Figure 1 illustrating discrete and continuous data flows. Table 1 is relocated beside training/results prose, while Table 2 becomes a wider display with an additional comparator column.

improvement.justification: V2 makes scalar handling more explicit and unified, removes direct scalar-magnitude dependence from attention, and adds evidence for a shared multitask processor. Its expressivity and convergence caveats better qualify the central claims. The gain is limited by prose-only reporting of multitask success and the loss of explicit per-task state descriptions, which makes the modified hints less self-contained; existing tabulated scores provide no additional performance improvement.
